papers.authors: Zhijing Shao, Zhaolong Wang, Zhuang Li, Duotun Wang et al.
papers.what: [Conference] We present SplattingAvatar, a hybrid 3D representation of photorealistic human avatars with Gaussian Splatting em-bedded on a triangle mesh, which renders over 300 FPS on a modern GPU and 30 FPS on a mobile device. We disentangle the motion and appearance of a virtual human with
papers.summary: We present SplattingAvatar, a hybrid 3D representation of photorealistic human avatars with Gaussian Splatting em-bedded on a triangle mesh, which renders over 300 FPS on a modern GPU and 30 FPS on a mobile device. We disentangle the motion and appearance of a virtual human with explicit mesh geometry and implicit appearance modeling with Gaus-sian Splatting. The Gaussians are defined by barycentric coordinates and displacement on a triangle mesh as Phong surfaces. We extend lifted optimization to simultaneously op-timize the parameters of the Gaussians while walking on the triangle mesh. SplattingAvatar is a hybrid representation of virtual humans where the mesh represents low-frequency motion and surface deformation, while the Gaussians take over the high-frequency geometry and detailed appearance. Un-like existing deformation methods that rely on an MLP-based linear blend skinning (LBS) field for motion, we control the rotation and translation of the Gaussians directly by mesh, which empowers its compatibility with various animation techniques, e.g., skeletal animation, blend shapes, and mesh editing. Trainable from monocular videos for both full-body and head avatars, SplattingAvatar shows state-of-the-art ren-dering quality across multiple datasets. Code and data are available at https://github.com/initialneil/SplattingAvatar.

papers.title: Arithmetic Models for Commodity Futures, Vanilla, and Calendar Spread Options
papers.authors: Malthe Rauh Johansen, Nina Lange, David Skovmand
papers.what: [Explore] We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including
papers.summary: We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including calendar spread options. These properties make the model suitable for large-scale empirical estimation. We estimate the model using an unscented Kalman filter on a panel of WTI crude oil futures, vanilla options, and calendar spread options spanning 2013-2024. We find that three stochastic volatility factors are needed to capture both the level and slope of the volatility term structure, and that hedges based on these factors remove almost all of the daily risk of a portfolio of vanilla options. Calendar spread options provide information about the dependence structure of futures prices that is not captured by futures and vanilla options alone. A model estimated without calendar spread options systematically overprices them by overstating the decorrelation between adjacent futures contracts. Including these options in the estimation brings the model's decorrelation close to the observed decorrelation, which removes the overpricing and improves their hedges, at only a small loss of accuracy in the pricing and hedging of vanilla options. Finally, we show that the arithmetic model fits futures and vanilla options better than its geometric counterpart and hedges the vanilla options slightly better.

papers.title: Digital Nudge Effects in Optimal Stopping Games: Antagonistic Interactions in Layered Choice Architectures
papers.authors: Batisse Manhardt, Ja-Nae Duane
papers.what: [Explore] Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping b
papers.summary: Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping behavior and outcome quality in a sequential decision task. Using a 2^3 between-subjects factorial design grounded in the secretary problem (N = 181), we find that (1) an anchor nudge significantly increased exploration rather than constraining it (b = 1.207, p = .017); (2) the salience nudge produced the smallest effect of any condition; and (3) combining the anchor and social proof nudges produced the worst outcome quality of any condition ($181.83 vs. $192.21 for anchor-only), with outcome quality declining monotonically as nudge count increased. These findings provide the first controlled evidence for a digital nudge crowding-out effect with direct implications for the ethical design of digital interfaces.

papers.title: Central Limit Theorems for Optimal Transport Functionals
papers.authors: Haruki Kono
papers.what: [Explore] We establish central limit theorems for empirical plug-in estimators of scalar functionals of quadratic optimal transport maps and potentials, including Wasserstein costs and several risk measures constructed from transport-based multivariate quantiles. We study the one-sample pr
papers.summary: We establish central limit theorems for empirical plug-in estimators of scalar functionals of quadratic optimal transport maps and potentials, including Wasserstein costs and several risk measures constructed from transport-based multivariate quantiles. We study the one-sample problem with a known reference distribution and i.i.d. observations from the target distribution. A natural approach is to combine a limit theorem for the empirical transport map with the functional delta method. We show, however, that in dimensions at least two, empirical transport-map errors admit no nonzero weak limit in $L^2$ under any normalizing scale. Instead, we linearize the functional directly in the target distribution, obtaining an influence-function expansion with a remainder controlled by the transport-map error. The influence function is characterized by a linear elliptic partial differential equation. Under regularity conditions, we use this expansion to prove central limit theorems in low dimensions and establish validity of the empirical bootstrap. We also derive semiparametric efficiency bounds and show that the plug-in estimators attain them under the same conditions.

papers.title: SPECTER: Covert Data Exfiltration from Air-Gapped Systems via USB Power Modulation
papers.authors: Hyeongjun Choi, Ji Hyuk Jung, Ji Won Yoon
papers.what: [Explore] We present SPECTER, a post-compromise covert channel that uses host-side USB power control to exfiltrate information from air-gapped and network-segregated systems. A transmitter with administrative privileges encodes bits through USB power-management or device-state operations w
papers.summary: We present SPECTER, a post-compromise covert channel that uses host-side USB power control to exfiltrate information from air-gapped and network-segregated systems. A transmitter with administrative privileges encodes bits through USB power-management or device-state operations without placing the payload in USB data transfers. The resulting signals are recovered through three alternative receiver paths based on smartphone charging states, visible peripheral behavior, and near-field RF activity. Experiments on Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22.04 demonstrate the channel on commodity hardware, with charging-state signaling at 0.2-0.25 bit/sec across Android and iOS devices and peripheral-state signaling at 1.0 bit/sec using a USB mouse on Windows. RF reception is demonstrated using a software-defined radio with a loop antenna in direct contact with the USB cable. Channel availability and observable side effects depend on the host configuration, connected device, and receiver path. These results identify host-side USB power control as a mechanism for low-rate exfiltration of short secrets and motivate treating USB power-management and device-state events as security-relevant telemetry.

papers.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
papers.authors: Guillermo Badia, Carles Noguera, Gaia Petreni, Alice Portone et al.
papers.what: [Explore] We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Grädel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-orde
papers.summary: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Grädel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.

papers.title: The Labor of Storytelling: How People with Chronic Illnesses Leverage AI and Communities for Narrative Translation
papers.authors: Drishti Goel, Koustuv Saha, Martez Mott, Denae Ford
papers.what: [Explore] The distinctiveness of people with chronic illness as storytellers is how they experience their illness. Symptoms, pain, and biological disruptions are eloquent forms of speech of the body that beget social articulation. The stories people tell about illness shape how suffering i
papers.summary: The distinctiveness of people with chronic illness as storytellers is how they experience their illness. Symptoms, pain, and biological disruptions are eloquent forms of speech of the body that beget social articulation. The stories people tell about illness shape how suffering is legitimized, and acted upon. Large language models have emerged as new mediators within this landscape---a role once predominantly supported by communities. In doing so, these systems participate in what we term narrative translation: transforming lived illness experiences for particular audiences and purposes. Through 21 prototype-driven semi-structured interviews with people with chronic illness, we contribute an empirical account of how participants navigate this mediation alongside existing sources of support. Our findings surface distinct yet complementary roles participants envisioned for AI and their communities, and how trust in AI was shaped by learning model-boundaries and perceiving understanding. We characterize these findings to inform future designs of AI-mediated narrative support.

papers.title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
papers.authors: Christian Meske, Tobias Hermanns, Florian Brachten
papers.what: [Explore] Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

papers.title: Latency-Neutral Passive Cyber Monitoring for Grid-Edge Operational Technology Networks
papers.authors: Damian Byrne, Emad Abukhousa, Jason Reed, Saman Zonouz
papers.what: [Explore] Deterministic industrial networks often present an operational trade-off between maintaining microsecond timing of primary control loops and capturing security telemetry. This work investigates the engineering feasibility of the Operational Technology Supervisor (OTSV), a three-t
papers.summary: Deterministic industrial networks often present an operational trade-off between maintaining microsecond timing of primary control loops and capturing security telemetry. This work investigates the engineering feasibility of the Operational Technology Supervisor (OTSV), a three-tier passive monitoring framework designed to resolve this visibility challenge within timing-sensitive grid-edge infrastructure. By utilizing a Layer-3-unconfigured passive ingestion mode on bare-metal hardware via a physical switched port analyzer (SPAN) loop, the deep packet inspection engine is isolated from the production network, implementing a software-enforced unidirectional export policy. Performance validation conducted over a continuous audit comprising 32,927 active-monitoring round-trip time (RTT) samples yielded stable latency distributions across a laboratory power-monitoring loop running Modbus TCP and IEC 61850 MMS protocols. The measured latency delta between the unmonitored baseline and the active monitoring state was less than 0.12 milliseconds, supporting the feasibility of continuous high-fidelity security observation alongside stringent grid-edge metering timing bounds without measurably degrading the monitored reporting path.

papers.title: KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines
papers.authors: Soobin Cho, Gyuyeong Kim
papers.what: [Explore] Distance scans in partition-family approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search are typically limited by memory bandwidth. Existing systems therefore improve throughput by reading fewer bytes per candidate, often at the cost of recall. We present KatoANN, a CPU ANN search system tha
papers.summary: Distance scans in partition-family approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search are typically limited by memory bandwidth. Existing systems therefore improve throughput by reading fewer bytes per candidate, often at the cost of recall. We present KatoANN, a CPU ANN search system that removes this tradeoff by batching distance scans on Intel AMX, a CPU matrix engine. Batching allows multiple queries to reuse each fetched vector code, shifting the scan from memory-bound to compute-bound and enabling near-exact distances at the speed of a lossy scan. KatoANN stores each vector once as a 16-bit SQ16 code split into high- and low-byte planes. Its adaptive rank-then-refine scan first ranks all candidates using only the high byte, then refines a small survivor set using the full-byte code. Both stages use the same representation, avoiding a second copy of the raw vectors. Experiments across diverse high-dimensional workloads show that KatoANN is the fastest partition-family ANN search system in our evaluation throughout the high-recall range.

papers.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
papers.authors: Amane Yamaguchi, Shohei Kamiguchi, Masashi Hamaya, Shigeo Yoshida et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them,
papers.summary: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/

papers.title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
papers.authors: Gennady Andrienko, Natalia Andrienko, Manuel Resinas, Stef van den Elzen et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for t
papers.summary: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

papers.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
papers.authors: Jinhao Hu, Bardia Mohammadi, Mofasshara Binte Rafique, Lars Henning Klein et al.
papers.what: [Explore] AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose C
papers.summary: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.

papers.title: A multiplier bootstrap score test for Tobit specification
papers.authors: Xuewen Li, Xiaojun Song, Xiaogang Wang, Feipeng Zhang
papers.what: [Explore] In this paper, we propose a simple score-based specification test for the Tobit regression model, implemented through a computationally efficient multiplier bootstrap. We test correct specification through the conditional moment restriction that the generalized Tobit residual has
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose a simple score-based specification test for the Tobit regression model, implemented through a computationally efficient multiplier bootstrap. We test correct specification through the conditional moment restriction that the generalized Tobit residual has zero conditional mean, and construct a feasible score-based empirical process using the integrated conditional moments approach, conditioning on the estimated index so that no smoothing or tuning parameter is required. We derive a first-order uniform representation of the feasible process, showing how its limiting behavior is affected by maximum-likelihood estimation of the structural parameter, and obtain the asymptotic properties of the corresponding Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistic under the null, fixed alternatives, and a sequence of local alternatives. Since the limiting null distribution is non-pivotal, $p$-values are obtained from a multiplier bootstrap that mimics the first-order representation and therefore captures the parameter estimation uncertainty. Monte Carlo experiments, including an unknown-scale design, an index-visible/index-invisible power study, and comparisons with existing specification tests, confirm accurate size and competitive power across a range of designs and covariate dimensions. Two empirical applications further demonstrate the practical utility of our approach.

papers.title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
papers.authors: Xiaoyu Gu, Yu Xi, Chencheng Wang, Zonghan Zhou et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guide
papers.summary: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.

papers.title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
papers.authors: Ma ZhenYao, Yue Liang, Jian-Qiao Zhu
papers.what: [Explore] Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for d
papers.summary: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

papers.title: On the Vulnerabilities and Data-Free Removal of Watermarks in Batch Normalization Layers
papers.authors: Elena Rodríguez-Lois, Fernando Pérez-González
papers.what: [Explore] Batch Normalization (BN) layers have become a common choice for embedding white-box watermarks in Federated Learning (FL), providing a simple and effective mechanism for model ownership verification and participant identification. However, previous works have focused on robustnes
papers.summary: Batch Normalization (BN) layers have become a common choice for embedding white-box watermarks in Federated Learning (FL), providing a simple and effective mechanism for model ownership verification and participant identification. However, previous works have focused on robustness against generic model modifications, leaving the security implications of this design largely unexplored. In this paper, we identify fundamental vulnerabilities of BN-based watermarking schemes and propose a practical data-free attack that exploits them. Experimental results on two representative FL watermarking schemes show that the proposed attack consistently removes the watermark with minimal impact on model performance, even without access to representative training data. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of evaluating DNN watermarking schemes under threat models consistent with Kerckhoffs's principle, rather than relying on security through obscurity.

papers.title: PhonoBridge: Error-Aware Phoneme-Mediated EMG-to-Text Reconstruction
papers.authors: Wen Qiu, Jiacheng Zhang, Xuanda Chen, Siqi Cai et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to
papers.summary: Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to-phoneme frontend and a large language model (LLM) backend for text reconstruction. The frontend is trained on paired EMG-text data that consists of channel-wise feature extraction, cross-channel fusion, and electrode embeddings. With phonemes as the intermediate representation, we expand the backend's training data by converting LibriSpeech transcripts into phoneme-text pairs without additional EMG recordings. To adapt the LLM to frontend noise, we introduce Error-Profile-Guided Augmentation (EPGA), which perturbs transcript-derived phoneme sequences according to error patterns estimated from frontend predictions, generating additional training pairs for the LLM. On the Open Vocabulary silent-speech dataset, PhonoBridge achieves 24.77% WER, outperforming the previously reported best of 28.27% on the same test split.

papers.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.authors: Masahiro Kaneko, Hiromi Arai, Timothy Baldwin
papers.what: [Explore] Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to re
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

papers.title: CAESAR: Mixed Reality Search-and-Rescue Platform for Cognitive Attack Evaluation
papers.authors: Mingyu Zhu, Jiangong Chen, Yu Liu, Hillmer Chona et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, c
papers.summary: Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, coordination, and decision-making, making them vulnerable to cognitive attacks that subtly distort visual feedback, virtual content, or system synchronization. While prior MR security research has examined individual attack mechanisms, evaluations are typically conducted in isolated or single-user settings, and there is a lack of standardized collaborative testbeds for systematic adversarial experimentation. In this paper, we develop CAESAR, an end-to-end multi-user MR framework for systematic evaluation of cognitive attacks in collaborative search-and-rescue training. CAESAR features a modular architecture that integrates four classes of cognitive attacks within a synchronized collaborative scenario and incorporates a multimodal data collection pipeline that captures behavioral, performance, and subjective measures under adversarial conditions. We conduct a controlled user study with an in-depth analysis of the latency-based attack, demonstrating measurable effects on task performance and user behavior while characterizing users' subjective experience under adversarial conditions.

papers.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
papers.authors: Dinithi Dissanayake, Yasith Samaradivakara, Hyung Woon Lee, Yadeesha Weerasinghe et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though
papers.summary: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

papers.title: SWatcher+: A Holistic Approach to Deploying Learned Cardinality Estimators in a Dynamic Setting
papers.authors: Yuxi Liu, Vincent Capol, Xiao Hu, Pankaj K. Agarwal et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Cardinality estimation (CE) is crucial in database query optimization. Although recent advances have improved accuracy, deploying machine-learned CE models in dynamic databases remains challenging due to data updates and workload shifts. Retraining can be costly, but existing pra
papers.summary: Cardinality estimation (CE) is crucial in database query optimization. Although recent advances have improved accuracy, deploying machine-learned CE models in dynamic databases remains challenging due to data updates and workload shifts. Retraining can be costly, but existing practices offer little guidance on when and how to update models, resulting in simple periodic retaining strategies that are suboptimal. We propose SWatcher+, a framework that adapts learned CE to dynamic workloads by monitoring data updates and query feedback. SWatcher+ selectively monitors high-impact subqueries for which wrong estimates lead to poor plan performance, and it proactively applies corrections to estimates during query optimization. This strategy enables immediate adaption to data and workload shifts without waiting for full model retraining, and carefully balances the cost and benefit of monitoring and adaption versus retraining. Our experiments show that SWatcher+ offers a better trade-off between query performance and overhead compared with existing approaches, making it a more practical solution for deploying learned CE in dynamic settings.

papers.title: CoGaussian: Open-Vocabulary Gaussian-based Collaborative 3D Scene Understanding
papers.authors: Om Shivam Verma, Shaya Farahmand, Lingjun Zhao, Lu Gan
papers.what: [Explore] Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative s
papers.summary: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
papers.authors: Carlo Ciliberto, Alessandro Rudi, Enrico Tassi
papers.what: [Explore] AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirecte
papers.summary: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

papers.title: NousDB - A Fast Query Engine for Semantic Analytics
papers.authors: Christos Tsapelas, Georgia Koutrika, Yannis Ioannidis
papers.what: [Explore] Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, result
papers.summary: Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, resulting in poor scalability and limited optimization. We present NousDB, a high-performance semantic analytics engine built on Apache DataFusion\cite{10.1145/3626246.3653368}.Through NousDB we propose an extended relational algebra with three semantic operators and formal algebraic properties that enable principled query rewriting and cross-operator optimization. We further propose a token-based cost model using equi-depth token histograms to optimize batch sizing under context-window constraints and provide statistical guarantees for safe batching. Experiments show that NousDB achieves up to $\times 86$ speedups with both local and enterprise LLMs, while leading competitors in token efficiency and accuracy. These gains extend to complex JOB and Stack workloads augmented with semantic operators, supporting both traditional and semantic analytics.

papers.title: MAPLE: Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration
papers.authors: Kelvin Aladum, Nisar Ahmed
papers.what: [Explore] Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that re
papers.summary: Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach that adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on observed geometric cues in the current partial map. MAPLE generates multiple plausible map hypotheses and evaluates visibility separately within each to estimate frontier gain, preserving differences in predicted visibility across hypotheses. Across KTH floor-plans and real-SLAM environments at multiple sensor ranges, MAPLE consistently improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive approaches. Its lightweight procedural construction enables predictive exploration with limited computational resources. Experimental results further show that more accurate map prediction does not necessarily produce better exploration, highlighting the importance of how predictions are represented and used in exploration decisions.

papers.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
papers.authors: Christoph Riedl, Fernando E. Rosas
papers.what: [Explore] When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emerg
papers.summary: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

papers.title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.authors: Zhiyue Xu, Xukai Wang, Zhiyuan Huang, Mingjie Zhan et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions
papers.summary: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.

papers.title: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Detection via Small Language Models in RAG Pipelines: nokast-secureRAG
papers.authors: Abhishek Rai
papers.what: [Explore] Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, where malicious instructions in retrieved content are mistaken for trusted input. We present nokast-secureRAG, a roughly 0.5B-parameter small language model tha
papers.summary: Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, where malicious instructions in retrieved content are mistaken for trusted input. We present nokast-secureRAG, a roughly 0.5B-parameter small language model that acts as a semantic firewall between retrieval and generation. It jointly evaluates the user query and retrieved context, classifying the pair as safe, suspicious, or malicious. The model is trained using a teacher-judge-student pipeline: a 35B teacher generates 5,233 examples across four attack families, and an independent 120B judge re-labels them, achieving 95.0% agreement before student fine-tuning. On a held-out in-distribution test set, the model achieves 0.994 detection recall at a 0.026 false-positive rate and a 0.006 attack-success-rate proxy, outperforming a regex baseline, a public prompt-injection classifier, Llama Guard 3 1B, and its untuned version. Prompt-Guard-86M reaches 0.900 recall but has a 0.690 false-positive rate. On a judgment-flip test, where the same sentence is benign or malicious depending on context, the model correctly classifies both cases 75% of the time, outperforming the compared baselines. Ablations indicate that retrieved context carries the main attack signal, while query-context consistency reduces false positives. Single-request latency is 293-404 ms, above the target of 100 ms, while amortized throughput latency is 37 ms under batching. On the external PoisonedRAG benchmark, recall falls to near zero, indicating that fluent fact-poisoning attacks lie outside the detector's instruction-consistency threat model. We report this limitation alongside the in-distribution results. The model, data-generation pipeline, and evaluation harness are released open source.

papers.title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
papers.authors: Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Ming Li et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own ca
papers.summary: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.

papers.title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ
papers.authors: Jing Wang, Yitong Yang, Hao Dou, Yaomin Wu et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response format
papers.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.

papers.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.authors: Mohammad Kachuee, Phu Mon Htut, Sheng Li, Nikolaos Pappas et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems furth
papers.summary: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.
